questions.question: Explain why a partnership keeps a fixed capital account AND a current account for each partner, and state what the agreement of Khumalo and Smit promises each partner before profits are shared.
questions.expected_answer: The capital account records each partner's permanent investment — Khumalo R500 000 and Smit R250 000 — and stays fixed, moving only on a formal contribution or withdrawal. This keeps the base for interest on capital and the profit-sharing ratio stable, and shows readers the partners' long-term commitment. The current account records everything that flows between partner and business during the year: interest on capital, salary, bonus and profit share credited; drawings debited. A credit balance means the business owes the partner; a debit balance means the partner has drawn ahead of earnings. The agreement promises interest on capital at 8 percent — R40 000 to Khumalo and R20 000 to Smit — salaries of R132 000 to Khumalo and R156 000 to Smit, a R12 000 bonus to Smit if the sales target is met, and the remaining profit shared two to one, the ratio of their capitals.

questions.question: Give the double entries for the two adjustments new to this grade — creating and later adjusting the provision for bad debts, and capitalising interest on the loan — and trace the loan balance through the year.
questions.expected_answer: Creating the provision: debtors are R64 000 and 5 percent is provided, so debit Provision for bad debts adjustment R3 200 and credit Provision for bad debts R3 200; debtors are then shown at R60 800. The next year the provision is adjusted, not recreated: debtors of R78 000 need a provision of R3 900, so debit Provision for bad debts adjustment R700 and credit Provision for bad debts R700 — only the movement touches profit; a decrease would be credited to the adjustment account as income. Capitalised interest: debit Interest on loan R22 000 and credit Loan R22 000, because the bank adds the interest to the debt and no money moves. The loan balance: opening R200 000 plus capitalised interest R22 000 gives R222 000, less the repayment of R45 000, closing at R177 000 — opening plus interest less repayments equals closing.

questions.question: Explain which year-end adjustments are reversed on 1 March, which are not, and why the reversal prevents the February electricity account of R2 340 from being counted twice.
questions.expected_answer: The four timing adjustments are reversed exactly: accrued expenses, prepaid expenses, income received in advance and accrued income — each moved an amount across the year-end boundary, so each is flipped on the first day of the new year. Depreciation, trading stock deficit, bad debts and the provision for bad debts are never reversed, because they record value permanently consumed or lost, not a shuffle between years. For the electricity: at year end we debited Electricity and credited Accrued expenses with R2 340. On 1 March the reversal debits Accrued expenses and credits Electricity, so the electricity account opens the new year with a credit of R2 340. When the bill arrives and the payment of R2 340 is posted as a debit, the account nets to nil for that bill — the expense is counted once, in the year it belongs to, satisfying the matching principle by structure rather than by the bookkeeper's memory.
